newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Drugs trade said posing big problem in Kazakhstan.
newsitem.headline: Drugs trade said posing big problem in Kazakhstan.

text.p: Kazakhstan has become a busy transit route for drugs from Asia's "Golden Crescent" and domestic production of narcotics is booming, the head of Interpol in the former Soviet republic said on Thursday.
"Kazakhstan is already a transit centre for narcotics going to Europe and a large producer of its own drugs," Bekzhan Karikbolov told a news conference in Almaty.
He said the use of drugs and drug trafficking was "the most painful issue" facing Interpol in the central Asian country.
Narcotics -- opium and its derivatives -- were streaming across the vast, Central Asian state of mountain and steppe from Afghanistan and Pakistan, he added.
There were regular armed clashes on the Afghan border guarded by Russian troops as couriers try to smuggle opium into the former Soviet republic of Tajikistan on the start of its journey west.
Karikbolov said up to 100 kg (220 lbs) of raw opium transit daily through Kazakhstan's porous borders, which ring a country five times the size of France.

Kazakhstan's post-Soviet police force is poorly equipped to battle well-heeled gangs of traffickers. Last year, police seized in Kazakhstan 16 tonnes of narcotics -- just seven percent of the estimated annual turnover of the country's drug trade.
Authorities here are alarmed by the country's own fast-growing domestic production of narcotics.
Hashish and marijuana are produced in large quantities in the Chu valley which sprawls across Kazakhstan's border with Kyrgyzstan.

But recently drug dealers have also flooded the local market with a large amount of a new, more potent drug -- ephedron -- made from a medical plant growing in Kazakhstan's spectacular Tien Shan mountains.
The burgeoning drugs trade in the republic of 16.9 million people is also fuelled by a growing number of addicts.
Karikbolov said there were 20,000 drug addicts registered in the republic but said the real number was probably at least five to 10 times higher.
Alma Yesirkegenova, Kazakh coordinator of the United Nations Drug Control Project in the region, said: "Unfortunately, we cannot say there is a serious government programme to fight this vice."
She added: "We have inspected many schools, and in all of them children already know what marijuana or hashish is and show interest in drugs. This is very alarming."
Karikbolov said the cash-starved health ministry has been forced to close the country's only specialised hospital for drug addicts.
